subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT LEVELS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in light of the recent unemployment statistics it is clear that the plight of unemployed Canadians is no better since the Government promise to create "jobs, jobs, jobs". Indeed, there are 167,000 more Canadians out of work now than there were last month.
Atlantic Canadians were hit with the news from the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council that the growth of the Atlantic economy will slow down this year and that unemployment levels will remain rather frightening. In addition to this distressing news, we are advised by Statistics Canada that the number of full time jobs fell by 48,000; employment declined by an estimated 6,000 in Newfoundland, by 4,000 in Nova Scotia, and by 11,000 in Alberta; 23,000 jobs were lost in the construction industry, and 26,000 jobs were lost in the trade sector.
A glance at the unemployment rates for some of our major cities shows devastating increases; St. John's, Newfoundland 17.1; Sudbury, Ontario, 16.5; Hamilton, Ontario, 10.4; and, yes, Mr. Speaker, in my own riding, the town of Glace Bay, it is in excess of 55 per cent. I would urge the Government, Mr. Speaker, to take its responsibilities seriously and put into effect job-creation programs now which will affect and assist the unemployed in creating meaningful jobs.

subsubtopic: SETTLEMENT OF CAN-CAR RAIL STRIKE AT THUNDER BAY, ONT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last evening members of the United Auto Workers Local 1075 ratified a collective agreement with Can-Car Rail of Thunder Bay, a subsidiary of the provincially owned Urban Transportation Development Corporation. The vote signalled an end to a 12-week strike which has been devastating for the workers and their families, and which was drawn out by the company's
attempts to reduce the work force drastically through contracting-out provisions in the collective agreement.
I am happy to say that the workers were able to prevent such job losses, and were also able to win, among other things, improvements to their pensions. In a community with over 19 per cent unemployment, it is a relief to all of us to see an equitable settlement to this problem. It is now important that all levels of Government get behind the company and the workers to ensure a long-term future for the plant.
During negotiations, UTDC withdrew a $60-million contract to build equipment for the City of Boston. This means at least 100 jobs over the next two years for this company and its workers. I call on the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) to contact the President of UTDC immediately to encourage it to re-award this contract to the Thunder Bay plant.
I also call on the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) to meet with officials of UTDC to negotiate a sizable order for double decker rail cars as a replacement for VIA's ancient rolling stock. Can-Car is the only Canadian company with experience in the production of such cars.

subsubtopic: ELBOW LAKE WORK CAMP IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, from time to time we read and hear about our correctional institutions. Two weeks ago I had the pleasure of accompanying the Solicitor General (Mr. MacKay) on a tour of the Elbow Lake work camp institution located in my constituency. I must say that I was very impressed with this institution's philosophy and physical lay-out. Elbow Lake is a minimum security S-2 institution, with a population of 50 inmates and 27 staff. It is located in the rural community area of Harrison Mills.
It seems that this institution's major philosophy is to instill a strong work ethic in the inmates. This is accomplished by allowing the inmates to participate in the institution's forestry program.
The forestry program which Elbow Lake employs is vertically integrated, in that every phase of logging, sawmilling, and stand treatment is involved to some degree. It is equipped to train men in the basic skills required in outside industry. An inmate should have readily marketable skills in tree stand treatment, logging, and sawmilling. Its client, the B.C. Forest Service, offers substantive employment to its inmates, creating

February 13, 1985
a valuable contribution to the community, while maintaining the aims and objectives of the Correctional Service of Canada.
This institution enjoys a very good working relationship with the Citizens Advisory Committee, which is composed of prominent area residents who have adopted a position of advocacy on behalf of Elbow Lake with various agencies in the community. I think this is truly an admirable model for the Correctional Service to follow. As a prisoner from this institution said in his letter to me, and I quote: "A work camp like this one is a God-send. I will go back into society with none of the bitterness usually fostered on inmates in regular prisons".

And who is responsible for this criminal negligence, if you will pardon the expression, with respect to the Canadian economy? None other than our Liberal friends who were in power for nearly twenty years.
Mr. Speaker, you will understand, and so will our Liberal friends if they are capable of doing so, that it is scientifically impossible and metaphysically unthinkable to rebuild in six months what this country has lost over the last twenty years. subsubtopic: OIL SHIPMENTS THROUGH NORTHWEST PASSAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) gave the go-ahead to Panarctic Oils Ltd. to proceed with its Bent Horn project. The Bent Horn field is located on Cameron Island in the Canadian High Arctic. While this is a small scale pilot project, it is significant and symbolic in that, for the first time, crude oil produced in the High Arctic will be shipped by tanker through the Northwest Passage to southern markets. This project will begin this summer, Mr. Speaker.
Of greater importance, however, is the standard of the ship which will be used to transport this oil. This House should be aware that the vessel scheduled to carry the oil south from Cameron Island this summer, the M.V. Arctic, does not meet the safety regulations of the Arctic Waters Pollution Prevention Act. While conversion work will begin on the ship during the winter, it will not be brought up to standard in time for this summer's planned activity. The Government, therefore, will be breaking existing safety regulations if it permits the M.V. Arctic to carry oil south from Cameron Island this summer.
To get around this problem, the ship's operator, Canarctic, is in the process of applying to Transport Canada for an exemption from the regulations. I think the Government ought to clarify its intentions immediately. It must respect the existing legislation and regulations. There must not be a shipping free-for-all in the High Arctic.

subsubtopic: UNITED CHURCH STATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, two years ago the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops released a document entitled Ethical Reflections on the Economic Crisis. The controversy it generated over the moral implications of government economic policies which left 1.5 million Canadians unemployed goes on today. The Catholic bishops have today been joined by the United Church of Canada which, in a statement released in Regina yesterday, condemned government policies which do not give first priority to our number one problem, unemployment.
The United Church has proposed a five-point program to solve the moral crisis of the Canadian economy. First is a fairer tax system that would see an end to the free lunches given to many upper income Canadians and corporations who pay no income tax. They also propose increasing the levels of social assistance so that no Canadian lives below the poverty line. They propose the Government undertake a serious full employment program as Sweden, Norway, Austria, and the
February 13, 1985

Province of Manitoba have done. They propose the Government reverse the policy of eliminating social programs to reduce the deficit. They also propose that we pursue a lower interest rate policy in Canada.
I am proud to say that each of these proposals has found a voice in this House through the New Democratic Party. Unless we heed these words of wisdom from the spiritual leaders of our country, our moral crisis will only worsen and Canada will become a less humane place in which to live.

subsubtopic: TRANSPORTATION OF STRANDED AIRLINE PASSENGERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, congratulations to VIA Rail for coming to the rescue of hundreds of passengers unable to fly from Metro-Toronto to Ottawa yesterday because weather closed the airport. Personnel at these stations and on the trains looked after the extra numbers with confidence, concern, and courtesy. But I have to ask what can be done to make these extra numbers be regular numbers for the railway? Obviously VIA has to be faster and more frequent in its service to compete with the airlines, but that raises the question of what we can provide to help it do that.
We need to give rail passenger service between major population centres far more priority than we have been prepared to do in the past. Metro-Toronto could not have its high quality transit service without a large provincial subsidy. The universally acclaimed GO train service, serving commuters from Pickering to Hamilton, could not operate without provincial aid. Giving VIA the same priority, in the Montreal-Toronto-Ottawa triangle it serves, would help not only one out of every
three people in Canada, it would also contribute positively to coping with the energy challenge of the future. That challenge does not confront us immediately because of the oil glut, but it will return and we now have to plan for that time and improve railway service between major population centres.

Washington, advised us that there are no current plans to deploy nuclear weapons in Canada. We learned today there are current plans. subsubtopic: INTERIM REPORT ON AFRICAN FAMINE RELIEF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to give a brief interim report on the Canadian response to the crisis of famine in Africa. Since November, nearly 500,000 individual Canadians have personally contributed money to African famine relief. The average individual donation has been $65 per person which, Sir, is double the amount normally contributed to non-governmental organizations. We are witnessing an unprecedented humanitarian response which continues in intensity and is made more remarkable by the difficult economic conditions in our own country.
Acting in that spirit, with unanimous support of Parliament I announced a special $50 million fund for Africa in November. The Government committed part of that fund to match the money donated by Canadians. Originally, it was projected that the matching portion of the fund would be limited to between $15 million and $20 million. As a result of the overwhelming public response, I am announcing today the Government's decision to increase the limit on matching by providing an additional contribution to the fund for Africa of $15 million.

subsubtopic: INTERIM REPORT ON AFRICAN FAMINE RELIEF
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: INTERIM REPORT ON AFRICAN FAMINE RELIEF
speechtext:
The system of matching was an important catalyst in mobilizing contributions by Canadian citizens and encouraging the co-operation of non-governmental organizations, and I am confident that a high level of contributions will continue, even though a firm limit has been now set on the matching portion of the fund for Africa.
The Hon. David MacDonald was appointed the Special Co-ordinator for the African Crisis. He will complete his original mandate on March 31 and is preparing a detailed report. That will be submitted in March to the Government and then to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence. I have expressed to the Chairman of that Committee my hope that Mr. MacDonald's report could be considered as a high priority so the Government can have the recommendations of both the Committee and Mr. MacDonald when we consider any further special steps Canada might take in response to the crisis in Africa, including measures to encourage the continuing direct involvement of individual Canadians.
I want to advise the House of some of the initiatives Canada has taken so far.

Food products valued at $6.5 million have been shipped to Ethiopa through the World Food Program.
February 13, 1985

In the next few weeks, additional food shipments worth $11 million will be sent to the three Sahel countries-Mali, Niger and Chad.
Additional grants of $6 million have been given to the Canadian Food Grains Bank to finance the shipment of 30,000 tonnes of food to the region of the Horn of Africa-including Ethiopia-and Sahel.

A grant of $3 million for UNICEF is targeted specifically at health care for mothers and children and the development of long-term nutritional and sanitary service measures.
I want to stress that this is in addition to CIDA's regular Africa program which this year totals almost $300 million. Most of that money is directed to CIDA's programs that have longer-term objectives, aiming to assist African countries to become self-sustaining, particularly in agriculture. This is in keeping with the Canadian people's expectation that their generous contributions to African relief will be part of a lasting solution to these terrible recurrent tragedies that have been so wasteful of human life.

Keeping that objective in mind, I am pleased to announce that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has advised the president of the World Bank that, over the next four years, Canada will contribute $100 million to the World Bank's special voluntary contribution mechanism for sub-Saharan Africa. This new World Bank initiative will complement its regular program in Africa and is designed to help African countries make the necessary political and institutional reforms to boost their own production. To date, donor countries, including Canada, are committed to give about $1 billion in direct and additional contributions,

The heartening response by Canadians has been a lesson about sacrifice and generosity to all of us. This Parliament can be proud of its quick response to unparalleled suffering, but we should be more proud of and gratified with the response of thousands of individuals and groups across this country.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond to the statement by the Right Hon. Minister. First of all, we welcome the increase in the matching funds being made available. I think some clarifications are needed about the announcement and I want to ask a few questions.
Certainly Canadians have responded generously and I wonder why some arbitrary ceiling would be put on this generosity. It seems to me the Minister might consider that Canadians vote with their pocket-books. In so far as they are prepared to give, the Government ought to respond to that by removing this arbitrary ceiling.
I would like to ask very specifically about the $15 million. Is this a new $15 million which is being added, or is it being recycled from somewhere else? The previous speaker from the Liberal Party noted there were cut-backs in CIDA funding and IDRC funding. Is the Minister prepared to have those cuts restored? Some of those moneys taken out of one pocket and put into another pocket for emergency funding were otherwise destined to be spent in Africa on the very problem they have been diverted to. So it is not entirely new money, and if we want to talk about the generous response we are able to provide, we should be talking about new money, not just recycled money.
I would like to correct the impression given by the previous speaker that Canada has been the greatest per capita contributor. This is simply not the case. A number of western European countries have higher per capita donations, such countries as Holland, Norway and Sweden. I note with a certain amount of shame that Ethiopia was excluded from external aid by the previous Liberal Government for a number of years. This generosity is now making up for some neglect over a number of years.
Finally, I would like to ask the Minister to respond to the very precise list of needs compiled by Mr. Jansson, the UN co-ordinator for Ethiopia. Specifically, he asked for 1.3 million metric tonnes of food for this year. I suggest that a reasonable response for Canada would be in the order of 200,000 metric tonnes of grain. This is the area we have been asked to contribute to. There are other items on the list which Mr. Jansson has forwarded, but they can be provided by other countries. As a grain-growing country, this is certainly the contribution we ought to be making. I note that India last year provided 100,000 metric tonnes of grain, so when I suggest a figure of 200,000 tonnes it is not an unbelieveable figure. If a poor country which has experienced famine itself can be generous to the tune of 100,000 tonnes, why can we not afford 200,000? I would like to see a response in very precise terms on that, as well as on the question of restoring the funding which has been redirected to CIDA and IDRC.

For instance, did you know that Canadians now spend half their leisure time watching television? This means twenty-three hours a week watching television. The average Canadian will spend a total of nine years and his or her life watching television. It is also a fact that television as an instrument of social policy is very important for Canada, especially, Mr. Speaker, because of our geographical location along the American border, and the fact that 75 per cent of the television programs we receive in Canada are American.
Even now, with our national CBC channel, we are in a situation where our national culture is threatened by the fact that every day, Canadians are confronted with 75 per cent American content on television.
Mr. Speaker, before passing this Bill, we must ask ourselves: Is television a right that belongs to the Canadian people or is it a right that belongs to government and especially the Government in power in this Parliament?
Mr. Speaker, I would like to suggest that television is not the property of any government, either the former Liberal Government or the present Conservative Government. We are not here to exercise control over television. Television belongs to all Canadians, and Mr. Speaker, I shall, if I may, quote a former Canadian Prime Minister, a Conservative Prime Minister, who said that public television was very important for Canada.

I would like to point out to the House that a former Prime Minister, one whom I am sure Members on the government side of the House will well remember, R. B. Bennett, when introducing the Broadcasting Act into the House of Commons, stated that this country must be assured of complete Canadian control of broadcasting from Canadian sources free from
foreign interference or influence. He was unequivocal about the method. I think this is important in this new tone of private sector involvement which has come forth from this Government, and as well is the very real fear expressed by the Canadian people that if this particular motion is allowed to pass we may see public ownership of our public air waves being threatened as it never was before.
When Prime Minister Bennett introduced the Broadcasting Act, he told the Canadian people that no other scheme than that of public ownership can ensure to the people of this country, without regard to class or place, equal enjoyment of the benefits and pleasures of broadcasting. 1 do not think any government would be warranted in leaving the air to private exploitation instead of reserving it for the use of the people. That was the position taken by a former Conservative Government, and it was supported in later developments with respect to broadcasting when we heard from-
[ Translation]
-the Hon. Lionel Chevrier who is well known, particularly in Quebec, and who said: The main reason for promoting public television in Canada is that we would like to have popular and cultural programs produced in Canada, by Canadians and about Canada. Another issue is that somehow, if we support publicly funded television and radio, a public vehicle for cultural appreciation across the country, it will cost Canadian jobs. In terms of government expenditures in the arts and in the arts as an industry, the arts is one of the top 20 manufacturing industries in Canada. subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak on the amendments to the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission Act. I found myself agreeing wholeheartedly with the previous speaker, with the exception of one point. I am not sure that the people of Canada voted for the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) because they thought he would keep his promises. I think the people of Canada voted for the Prime Minister in unprecedented numbers because he was not a Liberal.
With respect to the Bill, I suggest that sometimes we forget that communications is a service for which the Government has a responsibility. Therefore, if we consider that our responsibility as a Government, then we should provide a minimum service which would be available to all people. When we are talking about communications-radio, television and telephone services-we should ensure that those services are available to as many people as possible and, as well, that they should be affordable to the general population.
In our wisdom, or lack of it, we in Canada have allowed a large portion of the communications system to be privately owned and operated for a profit. Profit is the aim of the operation. We have found it necessary in the past, and I am sure we will in the future, to regulate the industry in order to ensure that the services are available to all people at a minimum cost.
One of the great uniting factors in Canada has been the CBC, as was stated by the previous speaker. Other national systems have also contributed in the areas of radio and television, as has our well integrated and developed telephone system. My concern, which is shared by many Canadians, is that with the trend toward deregulation and the projection of a profit motive in the industry, we will be reducing the number of Canadians who have access to some of the services which have previously been available to them.
If we approach these national services in the way which is being suggested by the Government-not necessarily in this Bill, but generally in its philosophy-we will be making the communications services available at a cost which will make the profit more important than the service.
I would like to deal with three services which have been reduced because of the policies of this Government and the previous Government. The first area deals with services to the hard of hearing and profoundly deaf. The second area deals with the use and licensing of satellite dishes for television reception in remote areas, and the third area deals with the
suggested deregulation of long distance service with the introduction of CNCP into the market.
I would like to speak First on the hard of hearing and the profoundly deaf. Technology is in place for the hard of hearing to be able to use telephones. Telephone companies have suggested that it would be quite possible to make the required technology a part of every telephone in the country. That would make it possible for a person who is hard of hearing to use any telephone which is at their disposal. However, the CRTC decided that it would not make this technology available and that it would not force all producers of telephones in Canada to include it in the manufacturing of the instrument. We need to keep the kind of regulations in place which would ensure this kind of equality and allow hard of hearing people to be able to use the phone anywhere. Perhaps we should review this decision. Perhaps it should be looked at again.
Profoundly deaf people are able to use an instrument called the TDY to communicate over long distance, but it is a typing operation and is slower. It takes a lot more telephone time than an ordinary telephone call. Some telephone companies have recognized the extra burden of cost this would be to the profoundly deaf individual and have given these individuals a break in the area of cost, but others have not. The local telephone companies here in Ontario-although some low-cost break is given-do not provide the extra time for the profoundly deaf to use the telephone. Perhaps we should require that the telephone companies do that, but we can only do it by extended regulating by the CRTC.
I think we should recognize that in order to have a good communications service, it must be available to all people. For example, the areas of Canada which have been unable to access a lot of radio and TV programs are the remote areas of this country, the far north, parts of northern Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Alberta, northern British Columbia and northern Ontario. Because these radio and TV programs are not available to the people in those areas, many communities and individuals have sought to deal with this broadcasting disparity by purchasing and installing their own receiving equipment and rebroadcasting or otherwise distributing the signals on an unregulated basis. This seems like a very acceptable entrepreneurial solution to providing this service and I hope this Bill will seek to clarify the definition of such rebroadcasting facilities which are sometimes found in large apartment blocks and hotels. This Bill, I understand, will bring them all under the jurisdiction of the CRTC. However, for many communities in remote areas which have satellite reception and equipment and are not licensed, this legislation will cause problems.
Some Hon. Members of this House, including government Members, have made commitments to their communities that they would help these communities gain access to these television programs without intervention by the RCMP, as is happening now. In the case of remote areas and under-served communities, these problems are now being addressed-and I give the Government credit for this-by the task force on the
February 13, 1985

distribution in under-served Canadian communities of satellite received broadcasting services. This task force was supposed to report on February 11.
We in this Party support this Bill on the understanding that the Government will act quickly on the recommendations of the task force and that options will be implemented for increasing the level of service and reducing the cost to these under-served communities. We feel that the extension of regulations is important in ensuring the viability of the Canadian broadcasting environment.
We would recommend that two or three basic principles be included. First is the guaranteeing of availability of Canadian information and cultural programming across the country. That should be a standard we do not move away from but should increase where it is presently deficient.
Second, we should ensure that new measures are found to fill the needs of those in remote areas who are now discriminated against. That is the approach I think we should take. I hope the Government, in giving these powers to the CRTC, will recognize that the Bill as it now reads will cause problems for those remote communities which are presently using satellites to receive services which they otherwise would not.
The third area of concern, Mr. Speaker, is the possible results of deregulation of long distance rates. The possibilities of what might happen if we deregulate the cost of long distance rates have been well documented across Canada. We have a living example in the States where the increases have been substantial. If CNCP Telecommunications services is allowed to compete freely, it will decrease the long distance cost somewhat for people using the service.
It will decrease the cost of long distance telephone service, but who uses the long distance telephone service? The large corporations, a few individuals and businesses across Canada are the major users of long distance services. The deregulation of rates will mostly affect the greatest number of users. These are people who use the phone daily for communication with their family and so on. Local service will be increased greatly by the deregulation of the long distance rate. This has been well documented and put before the CRTC. There are some of us who believe the CRTC has no right to rule in this particular area, but that is another matter.
Deregulation in Canada is estimated likely to raise the local rates for telephone service between 70 per cent and 125 per cent depending on which province you live in. Ninety-eight per cent of Canadian households have telephones. Of these people, 25 per cent to 30 per cent live at close to the poverty level or below the poverty line. That means, Mr. Speaker, if we proceed with deregulation as requested by CNCP Telecommunications, 20 per cent to 30 per cent of the persons presently using their telephones may not be able to continue to do so because they will not be able to afford it. That makes the communications system of Canada no longer a service. It then becomes a profit-oriented operation which is not available to everyone in the country because of cost. As I mentioned before, Mr. Speaker, there are many of us who are not at all
CRTC Act
sure that the CRTC has the right to make a decision on this issue.
My last and final area of concern is that although the CRTC is a responsible body, the responsible organization for regulation of the telephone and broadcasting services, this country does not have in place a really viable communications policy. Therefore, there is no doubt that Canada needs a clear and articulated communications policy established by government. The CRTC should operate within that policy and make sure the service is provided to all Canadians.
In the last number of years, because the communications industry has grown like topsy, the CRTC has been forced to make decisions in areas where it has not made decisions in the past. This was done in the absence of policy from the former Government. I hope this Government recognizes that and brings forward a comprehensive communications policy within which the regulatory body, the CRTC, can work. If these changes have a tendency to increase the Government's tendency to privatization, then I think policy should be stated in terms which will protect people in remote areas and the lower level of income earners. These policies that I suggest the Government should place before this House should be made in light of fairness and service to all Canadians. We could support the Government in that kind of change in policy.

As I mentioned before, there are areas of my riding which are somewhat remote, there are very few sources of entertainment locally, so television and radio are very important to the people of my riding. There are farmers and fishermen who rely heavily on television and radio for their communications because of the local farm and fishing broadcasts which keep them up to date on weather conditions, market prices and general happenings in their industries. The CBC is one of the most important sources of this information in both television and radio formats. Basically, all the homes in Prince Edward Island listen to the Radio Noon program. It brings them reports on the prices of produce, fish, on research and development in those industries, and reports on developments which may affect their livelihood. Radio Noon is one of the major sources of information for these people, one that cannot easily be replaced. The local noon program in Prince Edward Island was eliminated with the Radio Noon broadcast from Halifax being substituted. Years ago we used to receive Halifax Radio Noon broadcast, but ratings in P.E.I. showed that only 5 per cent of the population listened to that program. However, when the program was moved to Charlottetown, ratings rose to 30 per cent. I was talking to some CBC employees just today on that very program and they say that in the last year or so the ratings have been up more than that. So I think the Islanders want to hear about their own industry and local events. It is difficult, of course, to get all the information locally, but Radio Noon, when it is returned to Halifax on April 1, will mean that a very valuable information source for all Prince Edward Islanders will be gone.
Window on Resources is of course another local television program covering the Island's primary industries, and that was eliminated in December. The primary industries of agriculture and the fishery are the very backbone of the P.E.I. economy. They deserve good local coverage. Soundings, which provides information to the fishing industry, has an uncertain future. Since part of the program is heard on Radio Noon, I am concerned about whether this program will report in the future.
Last weekend I had the opportunity to meet with one of the major farmers' organizations in the Province of P.E.I., the National Farmers' Union. Its members presented a brief on a number of issues pertaining to the agricultural community in P.E.I. The first item on the agenda was the cut-backs in programming and how it affected them. They made the point that these programs have done so much for their agricultural community. The Prince Edward Island Women's Institute is concerned about it because that was a vehicle for programming to get their message across. They were able to show what activities the Institute is carrying out on its own. Organizations such as the Maritime Fishermen's Union used that as an
information vehicle to get sound advice to the rural people. Mr. Wayne Easter, President of the National Farmers Union noted in this brief that nationally the CBC cuts will not be felt as greatly by farmers as they will be in the Atlantic region, and especially in Prince Edward Island. He pointed out that the amount of $75 million was a political decision. We must understand that it was within the Government's jurisdiction to make that decision. The CBC must decide how the cuts are to be exercised.
Other speakers here today mentioned some of the artistic programs that are involved, such as The Tommy Hunter Show and Don Messer's Jubilee which originated from Prince Edward Island. Those shows are part of our Canadian heritage. Almost every home in Atlantic Canada was taking full advantage of those shows. Another program which will go by the wayside is called Sounds of the Island. That is a winter program which is on once a week and which features local talent. There is nothing more attractive to rural Canadians than seeing someone from their own community perform. They feel good about that. They believe, and rightly so, that there is a lot of good quality entertainment which needs exposure through local programming.
When pay-television was introduced to Prince Edward Island, I received hundreds of letters from Islanders who were concerned about the quality of programming that could come into their homes and the effect it could have on their children and on all of society. Over the years, television programs have become more and more violent and more sexually explicit. With satellite dishes, cable television, and video recorders, television is becoming a centre of family life. Television has become a tool of education, and the characters portrayed on television have become role models to Canadians. When young people watch Hockey Night in Canada, they watch for the Wayne Gretzkys of hockey. When they watch Canadian football, they watch for the stars. In many cases young people pattern their lives after the so-called stars. In Canada we have some excellent sports figures. Every superstar, no matter what facet of life they represent or what occupation they pursue, becomes an idol to someone.
I am happy to see that this Bill addresses, to some degree, the quality of programming. The Bill states that:
-the programming provided by the Canadian broadcasting system should respect and promote the equality and dignity of all individuals, groups or classes of individuals regardless of race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability;
I am uncertain of how all of this will be achieved. I hope that Canadian programming will be maintained at a high standard without undue or unwarranted censorship. There is a very fine line between outright censorship and the protection that is outlined in this Bill. Further study of issues such as this will be required in committee in order to ensure that the rights of Canadians are not interfered with.
There is a significant Acadian population in my riding. I have received many letters from individuals and organizations who are very concerned about the effect that a 20 per cent
February 13, 1985

reduction in CBC's French operating budget will have on the future of French programming. It is difficult to maintain a minority language in a culture without significant support from communications sources such as radio and television. In the Acadian regions of my riding the French services provided by the CBC are the only French broadcasting services available. Any reductions in these services will have a very detrimental effect on the future of the French language and culture in Prince Edward Island.
On the local FM CBC station, La Maree de Vile provides an hour and a half of Prince Edward Island-directed programming five days a week. This program is relatively new and only came about because of pressures from the local francophone organizations, which have a great interest in the future of the French language and culture in Prince Edward Island. I hope to see programming such as this increased rather than eliminated.
I have received letters from individuals and groups concerned about the cut-backs to the Canada Council. These cut-backs will affect the future of culture in Prince Edward Island as well as in the rest of Canada. They will also affect the employment of a great many Canadians. The Canada Council is closing its regional office in Moncton, which is the only office in the Atlantic provinces. The cancellation of the toll free telephone line to the Canada Council office will further affect the contact that the East Coast will have with the Canada Council and with other writers and artists across the country. Artists will lose their access to free financing and marketing advice. The Arts Advisory Board, which consists of representatives from all regions of the country, has been abolished. The loss of programs such as this threatens the direction of the arts community in Canada. It is important that arts be maintained as an alternative source of entertainment and employment for Canadians. The arts is a very important industry in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, first I enjoyed the talk given by the Hon. Member for Egmont (Mr. Henderson). I always
enjoy listening to his speeches in the House. The cuts that are being made in the CBC, I think the Hon. Member will agree, are the decision of the president and the Board of Directors of the CBC and not of the Government.
Second, over the Christmas break I had the opportunity to watch CBC almost exclusively. It has some excellent programs and I agree with the Hon. Member about that. One program I want to mention especially entitled The Tin Flute was broadcast over three evenings. During those three evenings the only time I saw any commercials was on the Friday night. On Wednesday and Thursday nights there was promo after promo after promo for the same programs. These promos were shown until you were so sick of seeing them that you wanted to throw up.
Does the Hon. Member not think that the CBC could be more aggressive in marketing its very excellent products, such as The Tin Flute and seeking commercials? I am told that CBC salesmen sit on their butts. They wait for orders instead of aggressively seeking commercials for the excellent and widely-watched programs.
I am a former broadcaster. I have broadcast for a CBC affiliate and for the private sector. The private sector is very aggressive and gets commercials. This is not so for the CBC. Does the Hon. Member not think that the difference made in cuts of public expenditures could be made up by aggressive salesmanship for commercial programs?

subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I cannot honestly say whether they can or cannot. I would hate to see the CBC become too commercialized. subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my intervention in this debate will be short. There are a few points, however, that I wish to put on the record.
First, it has dismayed me for some time how technological change forces governments to react. The legislation we have in front of us is a reaction. It was originally in most of its form introduced by the Liberals. That Bill was never passed, but now with some changes it has been reintroduced by the Conservative Government.
I am reminded of a committee meeting I attended around 1980. I was the critic for my Party on cultural events. I was relatively new to the ways of the House at that time. Illegal dishes were very much on everyone's mind. The then Minister
CRTC Act
in charge, Mr. Francis Fox, was threatening legal action. In this general setting, the committee met. I suggested to Minister Fox that technological changes were occurring that would greatly force changes in the objectives of our broadcasting legislation and the Broadcasting Act and that in no way was it possible for the Government to hold back and attempt to legislate technological change and innovation. I remember the Minister at the time pooh-poohed me. I suppose he was looking down at me who was then a new Member. He suggested that I did not know what I was talking about, that dishes were selling for around $100,000, were of a cumbersome size, and that outside of a few instances where they were being used, he saw no immediate danger of their being used on a massive scale. In fact, he suggested that it would take several decades before we would have to look at that problem. It has been less than five years and the size of dishes has indeed come down. They are much more attractive now. They are much smaller. The price of dishes is also coming down. I suggest that in the next number of years their size will further decrease, there will be greater mass production of them, and they will become cheaper and accessible to more and more people.
There are changes in technology. This is what broadcasting is all about or what was envisaged in broadcasting by the men and women who originally drafted the Broadcasting Act. It now gives Canadians access to channels from all over the world. The original intent of the Broadcasting Act to preserve a Canadian broadcasting system in order to maintain a Canadian cultural identity is now being threatened, not by any ideology or act of Parliament but by the technology which is becoming available. Unfortunately in this situation, as well as in many others, we have a technological imperative, which is that all governments do essentially is to react-they allow the change to occur, the crisis to be created, and then they try to fill up the holes with pieces of legislation.
When I was a new Member sitting for the first time on the committee dealing with communications and cultural events, I suggested that we really needed a new Broadcasting Act, that we had to rethink our whole notion of what is broadcasting, that we had to begin to anticipate the newer technologies which were being invented and innovated, and that we had to sit down with our political agenda to maintain a Canadian cultural identity in terms of what it meant, given the new technologies. I believe that what I called for in 1980 at that committee meeting is still very valid today. We need a new Broadcasting Act. We need some new definitions of what is broadcasting. The present legislation does not really cover it. All we have are CRTC decisions, which in essence have become policy decisions because there is a legislative vacuum and we have legislation which is inappropriate to contemporary realities.
I wish to reaffirm-and I believe most Members of the House feel the same way-that in order to maintain a unique Canadian identity, Parliament has a responsibility. First, it is in the national interest, as well as in our economic, social and cultural interests, to maintain a Canadian identity. We should

February 13, 1985
CRTCAct
not be swallowed up in the mass broadcasting cultural milieu which is being created south of the border. In order to withstand that very powerful magnetism, we need collective action as a nation. We need clear and distinct government policies which ensure a Canadian cultural identity supported by the arts and institutions such as the Canadian Arts Council and the CBC. These are essential instruments in maintaining our cultural identity.
Of course there will be a price to pay for this. There is no doubt about it. Some of the decisions the Government and Parliament will have to make are: How much are we prepared to pay, or how important is it for us to maintain that cultural identity? I believe that it is very important. Without a cultural identity we will eventually begin to lose our political and economic identity, as well as our economic and political freedoms. Cultural identity is just as important as economic and political freedoms. I am prepared to pay a price for that, whether it be $35, $40 or $50 a year because it is that important to me.
I agree with many government Members who were quick to point out some of the shortcomings within the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The CBC needs a bit of a shake-up. It has become like an old mother hen. There are folks in there whose creative energies have long gone. It needs some new excitement, some innovation and some new creative impulses. That Corporation needs some new blood, but cutting is not injecting new blood; it is just bleeding. We have to inject new blood. This does not mean that we should take blood out, because that weakens an important instrument which maintains our Canadian cultural identity. I do not believe the Government knows what it is doing. It has to sit down and rethink the nature of broadcasting and the meaning of technological change. It should rethink how it can best act in these changes to ensure the maintenance of the Canadian cultural identity and what it can do to change the CBC to make it more effective and attractive to the Canadian viewing audience so that it can maintain its audiences, not lose them to American programming.
These are not easy questions to answer. I am not saying that they are. This is why I reacted with horror to the simplistic solution of the Government to hack away at the CBC and somehow or other it would be able to set its house in order. That is irresponsible behaviour.
I am hoping for some wisdom on the part of the Government and some realization that CBC is important as a cultural institution, that the Canadian cultural identity is important, and that these matters should be handled with care and great consideration.
I do not dispute that our scarce resources, especially taxpayers' money, should be husbanded and managed carefully. I was as horrified as members of the Conservative Party when we saw the waste of previous Liberal Governments, but I find the Tory solution just as repugnant. Husbanding and preserving means that things should be done with a lot of consideration and care. I think what we have seen is blind chopping away rather than careful husbanding and preserving.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member dwelt for some time on the way in which the CBC was created. Could he tell us whether some of the cuts he mentioned in his speech will affect regional programming or jobs in the area which he represents?

subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Absolutely, Mr. Speaker. We in western Canada have always fought to have more regional broadcasting in Saskatchewan. That occurred under the Liberal administration as well. There was a tremendous push toward greater centralization out of the major offices in Toronto and Montreal. I know people in Regina within the CBC who had to fight tooth and nail to preserve some of the turf, so to speak, in western Canada.
They have had to cut programs. Some of those cuts were occurring because of the policies of the previous administration. The Tories have made a bad situation even worse. We are going to have even less local and regional broadcasting and programs than before.

subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to consult my colleague for his opinion on the effect of these cut-backs. He knows that investigative journalism within the CBC was cut with the encouragement of the previous administration, and, I presume, the management of the CBC. Investigative journalism groups, especially in CBC Radio, were instrumental in changing the face of Canada to some degree. A small group attached to CBC Sunday Morning was able to get spruce bud worm spraying cut in half in New Brunswick after doing detailed research into it. This investigative journalism research presented on CBC Sunday Morning over a period of three years won a battle for the atomic veterans of Canada. It is now understood that most of this money-and maybe my colleague can verify this-for investigative journalism within the CBC was drawn off into that big toothy grin of the program The Journal. Many of the programs have suffered. Now the whole CBC will be called into question. It is probably one of the finest organizations in Canada. The cut-backs will gut that organization to the bottom.
I know the Hon. Member is from a rural area. In many areas of this country, there is still no television. The only sort of intellectual stimulation and quality programming comes from CBC Radio. In my area, we receive radio signals from the United States such as Los Angeles much better than we do the CBC. Is it fair that the Conservative Government should encourage these kinds of deep cut-backs that would destroy the kind of quality produced by the CBC, especially the loss of investigative journalism as one example, and the failure to provide decent radio communication, in particular in the rural areas of Canada?

subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, indeed. I deeply regret the cuts, particularly in the area of investigative journalism. The CBC in Saskatchewan has played an important role, as part of the fifth estate, of being able to develop stories, develop issues and do the important job that good investigative journalism is
February 13, 1985

all about. The CBC in Saskatchewan has also had its scoops, so to speak, and has contributed to the well-being of the public as a whole in doing so.
As well, the cuts will affect rural areas, particularly areas in northern Saskatchewan. Native programming and northern programs are all under the axe. These are areas that are on the fringe, at least geographically, of mainstream Canadian society. These are the areas that really constitute the vast majority, in terms of geography, of this country. If we want to keep this country together, one of the essential threads in keeping that fabric together is the CBC.
When you start cutting out that thread, what you do is to increase the sense of isolation and the sense of alienation the different geographical sectors of this country will feel. Instead of helping to create a quilt of the many different parts that constitute Canada, you will loosen those ties which contribute to the sense of cohesion that we need in Canada in order to survive as a country and as a national entity.

subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have some comments on the very perceptive observations of the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong). He points out quite rightly that legislation lags behind technology. He points to the day when you will be able to buy for $25 a little instrument about the size of a cigarette package that you can stick on your windowsill which will enable you to tune in to any one of 250 satellites.
What this is going to bring to Canadians is freedom of choice. The Government in its wisdom, or lack thereof, will no longer be able to say, "There are four broadcasters operating in this area. We will insist that you carry so much Canadian content. We will tell you which programs you can broadcast and which ones you cannot". At that time, and the circumstances apply very much today in many areas, people will be able to turn off or tune in to whatever they want.
This will bring freedom of choice to Canadians. It means that the Government will not be able to dictate what people listen to or look at over television. If the Government or the people of Canada think it is important that there be Canadian content, the only way that will be possible will be to have programs that the people themselves want to listen to or watch.
I wonder whether there is a better way of ensuring that this happens than by putting a billion dollars or thereabout of public funds into the CBC to produce a broadcasting system which people very often choose not to listen to or look at. In the city I come from, the CBC spends a lot of money. The little local broadcasting station will pick up about 85 per cent of the listening audience on CBC. Might it not be possible to reallocate some of that billion dollars of public funds into some other mechanism whereby programs can be picked up by private broadcasters, the public funds can be used better, and proper Canadian content is ensured?

Mr. Speaker, one has no trouble realizing that the role which these various institutions play within Canada is appreciated by all Members of the House. The Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) indicated to two Members of the House that he wants to ensure that Canadians have freedom of choice. He wants to see an end to the day when the Minister of Communications, or another Minister of the Government of Canada, can dictate to Canadians what they should watch. I think it is fair to say that 85 per cent of the population of this country has complete freedom of choice, or as much freedom as can reasonably be expected, with respect to viewing television channels or listening to radio stations.
I am a bit worried, if the Hon. Member is suggesting that cutting back the CBC, funds to the National Film Board or the National Arts Centre to make those institutions more competitive and having the CBC compete against other networks will somehow improve the means of communication in Canada. In a very large chunk of the country, including the area which I represent-the west coast of Newfoundland and the great northern peninsula of Newfoudland and the western Arctic from which the Hon. Member hails as well as parts of

February 13, 1985
CRTC Act
western Canada, the citizens in many communities have no other communication option but the CBC. When we talk about the billion dollar budget of the CBC and make comparisons between the CBC needs for that money to provide the nation with a national network and CTV or Global-TV being able to do it for less, we are forgetting that there is only one communications network in the country that has a mandate, responsibility and obligation to provide television in every community which has over 500 people from one end of Canada to the other. CBC is also the only radio network that has the obligation and responsibility to provide programming from one end of Canada to the other.
It is a bit short-sighted and nefarious to say that, because the CBC is approaching a billion dollars in spending, it must necessarily be fat. The CTV is not providing programming in the great northern peninsula of Newfoundland, the Port au Port Peninsula of Newfoundland, the south coast of Newfoundland or the Bay of Islands of Newfoundland. In fact, a large number of rural regions in Canada do not receive programming from CTV, Global-TV or private radio networks. The reason is simple. The private networks are licensed and regulated by the CRTC, but they are quite rightly in the business of making a buck. If there are not advertising dollars to justify providing television signals across 500 miles of rugged coastline on the northern peninsula to 30,000 people, then those networks will not be there. But the CBC, with its so-called fat budget, is there because it has to be there. It does not make money providing a signal to Labrador, to the great northern peninsula, the Port au Port Peninsula, the Gaspe, northern New Brunswick or the western Arctic. But it is there. It is the only network in the country which ensures that Canadians, no matter where they live, can be assured of a basic service. Therefore, it is a fundamental mistake to stand in the House and talk about the CBC in terms of its efficiency versus that of the private networks. It is in a totally different business.
I have had the pleasure and the honour of working for both the CTV and the CBC networks. There is no question that in some regions CBC is better outfitted, that its equipment is more modern and its facilities are up to date. However, when I worked for CTV in the Province of Newfoundland, with the budget we had, we tried to put on the best news casts we could provide. We were not concerned about whether or not St. Anthony had a reporter or whether any of the reporters ever saw St. Anthony, Newfoundland. In fact, the CTV network today, in a province as rural as Newfoundland, including Labrador, has one team of reporters in the capital city of St. John's. By contrast, CBC has stations in St. John's, Grand Falls, Corner Brook, Labrador City and Goose Bay. Members may not appreciate that, but I am attempting to point out that on a per capita basis CBC spends much more money in providing the service to the people of Newfoundland. Everybody in Newfoundland receives equal service, which is not the case when a private network is involved.
The Hon. Member for Western Arctic suggested that if CBC wants to maintain its share of the market it must
compete on an entertainment basis and that it must provide an equal entertainment value for people to make a choice. When Canadians are given the choice between Canadian-produced programs and American produced programs, they respond dramatically and watch the Canadian-produced programs. The national news reaches 1.8 million people in the country on most week nights. The Journal reaches 4 million Canadians per week, with almost 1.6 million people watching every night. The Fifth Estate reaches 1.5 million people. Fraggle Rock reaches 1,600,000 Canadians. Canadians are responding to Canadian-produced programs. But if we think that we are going to change CBC, the Canadian film industry or the National Film Board, or enhance Canadian culture without first doing an analysis of what is required within the industry, and understanding the ramifications of cutting dollars to the Canadian film industry and how those dollars ripple down through what is still a very fragile industry, then I am sorry because that is not the way to do it.
We should not forget that we share a border with a fascinating neighbour to the south which has a population of 250 million people. The United States has very well established and well oiled broadcasting film and entertainment industries. In Canada we have only begun to make headway in recent years. If we think that by cutting back we will make the Canadian industry more competitive, then I am sorry. I share with Members opposite the concern that we must ensure that we get a better bang for our buck with respect to the current budget of the CBC. I also share the belief that we can get much better value for our dollars from the CBC. I believe as well that it is not being irresponsible to suggest that there is fat within the CBC to be cut, particularly on the administration side, but I do not think that having the Minister, one month after the election, start by arbitrarily picking $85 million out of the air and having a panic reaction as to where cuts should be made within the organization, is doing any kind of service to the people of our country.
My riding has a population of 90,000 people. My constituency has 500 miles of coastline, and over 50 per cent of its communities have a population of under 1,000 people. It is difficult enough to try to service that area and ensure that those Canadians living along the 500 miles of coastline have their right to be heard, and have not only their problems aired but their aspirations reported, not only in their own home province but across this nation. The CBC has one station in the City of Corner Brook. But when these cut-backs were announced, arbitrarily and without proper consultation, what happened, Mr. Speaker? We were told that that station will have five personnel wiped out. If the 90,000 people in my riding lived in four city blocks, I would not be upset, but they do not, they live along 500 miles of coastline. That one station is now left with a handful of reporters who are trying to give decent coverage and representation to people who live all the way from Burgeo on the south coast to St. Anthony and southern Labrador in the northern peninsula. That is an impossible task, Mr. Speaker. For most Canadians who live in

urban settings and high-density population areas, access to media can be had as quickly as it takes to make a telephone call or to call a press conference. That is not the case for the people on the great northern peninsula, whose aspirations and problems are as legitimate as the aspirations and problems of someone living in Toronto, Vancouver or St. John's, Newfoundland. For my constituents to take advantage of their broadcasting system and their right to be heard, it requires making an appointment. In other words, if someone lives in St. Anthony, and if a newsworthy event happens, it gets reported a week later. If someone is anticipating something newsworthy occurring, an appointment has to be made with the CBC. That kind of situation can only worsen.
When I tell this kind of story about the CBC's mandate and the incredible cost of providing coverage to those areas, I am not speaking just about Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe or just about Newfoundland. The same is true in northern British Columbia, the northern provinces of western Canada and, indeed, in some parts of northern Ontario and Quebec. Canadians who live in my part of the country and resign themselves nightly to only one choice when watching television, namely the CBC, very often engage in a favourite pastime. It is called "cursing the CBC" My friend, the Hon. Member for Western Arctic smiles. But it needs to be said, Mr. Speaker, that even though they must watch the same programs night after night, the CBC is there providing the signal. The other private networks are not. Although these people get tired of watching the same channel, the programming nature of the CBC, whether it be regionally developed entertainment or news programs, at least makes it possible to see a reflection of themselves, their communities, their aspirations and, indeed, the problems they confront on a day-to-day basis. There is a very deep and abiding appreciation of the value of having the CBC, be it radio or television, in the northern areas.
When we look at the breakdown of the $85 million cuts being proposed for the CBC, we find the figures rather interesting. We see $30 million being cut from administration. I cannot comment on that. I do not think anyone in this House can properly comment on that. It seems a good area at which to target a cut-back because there has not been a proper debate or an impartial investigation. The Minister appointed loggers, axemen, to decide where the cut-backs are to be made. We see $15.5 million being cut from network programming, Mr. Speaker. What does that mean? It means that in the areas where Canadians can avail themselves of a dozen TV channels, there is a $15.5 million cut across the board. We see a $10.4 million cut from regional programming. What does that mean? It means that in those parts of this country where people cannot avail themselves of a dozen or two dozen different stations or channels, in those parts of the country where the only available network is CBC Radio or television, $10.4 million is slashed.
In the case of the riding of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker), it does not mean that they are going to lose two or three jobs at CBG Gander; it

means CBG Gander is closing outright. It means that the people who live in the great community of Gander in the area of Notre Dame Bay, the fishermen who depend upon the CBC to be heard, to get weather forecasts, cannot do so any longer. On the northeast coast of Newfoundland, the great historic fishing area of Newfoundland, the people no longer have access, except by long distance telephone, to any means of communication with people outside of their own rural-and I emphasize "isolated"-communities. That is what it means, Mr. Speaker. The $10.4 million cut means that for the people of Labrador West in the Towns of Labrador City and Wabush, where the Iron Ore Co. of Canada is located-which used to be run by a gentleman who has now gained a new distinction in this country-jobs have been lost. Mr. Speaker, as all Members know, certainly we on this side of the House have no intention of being partisan in the questions we ask. The Hon. Member has outlined very succinctly the difficulties with respect to the isolation faced by the fishermen of Newfoundland and how important it is for them to get signals from the outside. However, as an Ontarian who has often enjoyed the political commentary that we hear from Newfoundland on CBC Radio, I wonder if the Hon. Member could elaborate on what role the CBC has played, not only in getting information to Newfoundland but in getting the message of Newfoundland politicians out to the country at large.
I have often enjoyed the turn of phrase which has been utilized by my hon. colleague here today. I think this is a hallmark of debate and discussion in the legislature in Newfoundland. Certainly having had the pleasure in the past of hearing one of the great orators of all time in the person of Joey Smallwood, I think that kind of message has been disseminated largely through the radio programs of the CBC. Could the Hon. Member comment on whether he feels the CBC has played any role in getting Newfoundland's message out to other Canadians?

subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for her questions. They are most appropriate. There are two stories to be told. Not only has the CBC allowed Newfoundlanders the opportunity, which opportunity they have of course taken advantage of, to ensure that the threads which make up the Canadian mosaic include Newfoundland threads, but it has also allowed us to provide our own unique and distinctive flavour to this mosaic. As well, Newfoundlanders, because of the CBC facilities, have had a chance to communicate with each other on the Island. I think we often forget that until 1965 the people of Newfoundland were not even connected by highway. Until 15 years ago there were still large parts of the northeastern coast which had no road connections. In my own riding, the great northern peninsula has been accessible by road only in the last 15 years. So the role of the CBC has been important in terms of sharing our thoughts and views with our fellow Canadians, as well as those other things which make us distinct and unique and, I hope, interesting.
The CBC has also provided Newfoundlanders with the chance to talk to each other. Some great and very popular cultural organizations have grown out of the facilities provided by the CBC. I think of the wonderful Grand Band in Newfoundland and some theatre groups like Codco and Rising Tide Theatre, one of which was here just a few years ago with the play Joey which sold out at the National Arts Centre. Incidentally, this is another organization subjected to severe cut-backs as outlined by the current Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse).
I said earlier that as a Newfoundlander I am not inward looking about the effects of these cut-backs on my province only. I know the story which can be told about the cut-backs in Newfoundland, the effect on fishermen and people in the forest industry, as well as the thousands of fishermen on boats at sea who depend upon the fishermen's broadcast every night
to stay in touch with their families, receive messages and find out what the weather is going to be. I know that story can be told all across this country and I do not think we have taken a sufficiently serious and hard look at what the impact will be before we rush ahead with simply cutting dollars. We have also wrongly been comparing CBC service with that being provided by private networks. The private networks are wonderful, God bless them, but they are not in St. Anthony, not on the bill of Cape St. George, and they are not in the Western Arctic. CBC has that mandate and it is expensive programming to provide.
